name: Endowment effect
aliases: Willingness to accept-willingness to pay disparity
statement: People demand more to give up something they own than they would pay to acquire it, so goods handed out at random tend to stay where chance put them.
meaning: Two experimental paradigms carry the name, and they do not measure the same thing. In the valuation paradigm one group is given a mug and states the lowest price at which it would sell, while another group states the highest price it would pay. The gap between the two is reported as a ratio of willingness to accept to willingness to pay. In the exchange paradigm everyone is handed one of two items of similar value and offered a swap. If ownership carries no weight, about half should trade. Loss aversion is the usual explanation for both patterns, and it is an explanation rather than the observation. The endowment effect is a measured asymmetry between owners and non-owners; loss aversion is a claim about the shape of a value function. This site keeps them in separate entries because the evidence for each is separate, and the coefficient argument belongs to the other one.

origin.where: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
origin.note: "Toward a positive theory of consumer choice" names it in one line: "Henceforth, I will refer to the underweighting of opportunity costs as the endowment effect." Thaler's evidence was three anecdotes and a pair of survey questions about a fatal disease, to which a typical answer was $200 to buy a cure and $10,000 to accept the same risk. He wrote that aside from Kahneman and Tversky's survey data there was "little in the way of formal tests". The laboratory demonstrations came a decade later.

evidence: Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler ran the experiments the name now travels with. They first traded induced-value tokens, where each participant was told what the token was worth to the experimenter. Those markets cleared at the predicted volume, a ratio of actual to predicted trades of 1.0. The same people, under the same rules, then traded coffee mugs and pens, and the ratio fell to about .31 on average. In their experiment 5, with 29 potential buyers and 30 potential sellers, 14.5 trades were expected and six occurred. The median selling price was $5.75 against a median buying price of $2.25, with means of $5.78 and $2.21. Experiment 6 added a third role. Seventy-seven Simon Fraser students were made sellers, buyers, or choosers, who picked between a mug and cash at each price. Median valuations were $7.12 for sellers, $3.12 for choosers and $2.87 for buyers. Experiment 7, with 117 students at the University of British Columbia, gave $7.00, $3.50 and $2.00. Sellers and choosers face objectively identical options, which rules out an income effect and locates the gap on the selling side. The exchange design comes from Knetsch in 1989. List describes that paper as finding 89 percent of those given a mug kept it, and 90 percent of those given a chocolate bar kept theirs. The 1989 article carries no DOI and was not opened for this entry, so those two figures arrive at one remove. Horowitz and McConnell later pooled 201 experiments and put the mean ratio of accept to pay at 7.17, standard error 0.93, with a median of 2.60.

replication.headline: Plott and Zeiler made the gap vanish in 2005 by tightening the elicitation procedure, and a 2015 study running those same procedures found a ratio of 2.53 for mugs.
replication.detail: Plott and Zeiler argued that the gap is an artefact of subject misconceptions about the mechanism used to elicit values. Their 2005 procedures added anonymity, an incentive-compatible mechanism and paid practice rounds before any mug was valued. Their abstract states the result: "Using the modified procedures, we observe no gap between WTA and WTP." A 2007 paper applied the same reasoning to the exchange paradigm and reported no asymmetry under modified procedures and its reappearance under traditional ones. The full text of the 2005 paper could not be opened during this check, so no number from it is quoted here. Isoni, Loomes and Sugden replied in 2011 that unpublished lottery data from the same 2005 study showed a disparity that persisted, and reported new evidence for both patterns. Plott and Zeiler answered in the same issue that all the mug data reject endowment effect theory and that lottery gaps come from shifting beliefs about the lotteries. Fehr, Hakimov and Kübler then ran the Plott and Zeiler protocol at the Technical University of Berlin with 191 students, 95 in the mug sessions and 96 with a USB stick. Mean willingness to pay for the mug was 1.34 euros against a mean willingness to accept of 3.39 euros, a ratio of 2.53 (t = 5.01, p < 0.01). The USB stick gave 3.54 against 5.60 (t = 4.08, p < 0.01). They then used dominated bids in the practice lotteries to find the people who plainly understood the mechanism. The 42 of 95 who never bid outside the bounds on any of the 16 lotteries still gave 1.48 against 3.02, a ratio of 2.04, p < 0.015. Their conclusion is that misconceptions are not the main source of the gap. In the field, Fehr and Kübler embedded the exchange design in the German Socio-Economic Panel, handing 3,146 respondents either a towel or a notebook and offering a swap at the end of the interview. The overall trading rate was 32 percent, 38 percent among those given the towel and 28 percent among those given the notebook, against a benchmark near 50. Trading was unrelated to their measure of loss aversion, and telling people in advance that a swap would be offered changed nothing.

study.cite: Fehr, D., Hakimov, R., & Kübler, D. (2015). The willingness to pay-willingness to accept gap: A failed replication of Plott and Zeiler. European Economic Review, 78, 120-128.

limits: The effect belongs to inexperienced traders more than to people in general. List took the exchange design to the floor of a sportscard show and ran it on 148 people, 74 dealers and 74 non-dealers. Dealers traded at 43.6 and 45.7 percent across two designs, close to the 50 percent benchmark, while non-dealers traded at 20 to 25 percent. Splitting the non-dealers at their mean of 5.66 trades a month sharpens it: 14 of 30 experienced non-dealers traded, 46.7 percent, against 3 of 44 inexperienced ones, 6.8 percent. List reports that market experience rather than selection drives the difference. No multi-laboratory preregistered replication of either paradigm was located. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex and the open web returned none, and the closest thing is the Fehr and Kübler field experiment, registered as AEARCTR-0003992 and still a discussion paper rather than a journal article. Two figures here were read off versions other than the ones usually cited. The Horowitz and McConnell numbers come from the August 1999 University of Maryland working paper; the 2002 journal article is paywalled and was not opened. Gächter, Johnson and Herrmann's 2007 discussion paper reports a sample of 360 and their 2022 journal version reports 660, so only the published figure is used here.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat a mug result as a measurement of loss aversion. Gächter, Johnson and Herrmann elicited both from the same 660 customers of a car manufacturer. Their published abstract reports that riskless and risky loss aversion are strongly positively correlated, and that riskless loss aversion is higher on average. Correlated is not identical, and a valuation gap constrains the coefficient only loosely. The second error is quoting 7.17 as the size of the endowment effect. It is Horowitz and McConnell's mean across every kind of good, and it is pulled up by public and non-market goods at 10.41 and health and safety at 10.06. Ordinary private goods, the category mugs and pens sit in, average 2.92, and the median across all 201 experiments is 2.60. The third is reading Thaler's coinage as a claim about attachment to possessions. He defined it as the underweighting of opportunity costs, which is a claim about how a forgone gain is booked rather than about affection for an object. The fourth is treating Plott and Zeiler as having settled the question. Their argument is about experimental procedure, it was contested inside the American Economic Review by Isoni, Loomes and Sugden, and the one published attempt to repeat their protocol found the gap intact.
